reviewed: All boards together: ASIC boards top and bottom V7 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 00:07 CST; FPGA-LDO A layout V16 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 09:49 CST; Frontend 14 layers V7 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 11:15 CST; HDMI Extension Board V37 · edited 10 Nov 2026, 13:36 CST; pin map V6, frozen 13 Nov 2026, 08:36 CST
readiness: Not ready to order: 4 items must be settled first.

findings.title: PCBWay has not confirmed ten layers in 0.8 mm for the ASIC boards.
findings.why: Ten layers in 0.8 mm is outside PCBWay's standard range (https://www.pcbway.com/capabilities.html). If PCBWay refuses, the thickness, vias and stack height all change. The fit and print models already use 0.8 mm (set V3, 13 Nov).
findings.action: Send the ASIC V7 stack and via table to PCBWay and get a written yes for ten layers in 0.8 mm with ENEPIG and laser vias.

findings.title: The ASIC designer still owes the die and bond-loop height, the capacitor values and the VDD_CGEN level.
findings.why: The bonded dies sit about 1.5 mm under the next ASIC board. If die, bond loops and encapsulant exceed about 1.4 mm (less with tall back-side capacitors), mating the next board crushes the bond wires. VDD_CGEN is supplied at 1.5 V; the earlier LDO design used 1.6 V. The ASIC board J3/J4 have no part number, so a taller DF40 could also be fitted.
findings.action: Get die thickness, loop height, encapsulant height, capacitor values and the VDD_CGEN level from the ASIC designer; record a maximum height. Put the DF40 part numbers on ASIC J3/J4.

findings.title: Panel break-off tabs sit beside mating parts on the Frontend and FPGA-LDO A.
findings.why: The Frontend's south edge is 0.567 mm from the near ASIC board, and its panel puts two tabs on that edge; a tab nub can stop the 0.45 mm DF40 engagement. Four of FPGA-LDO A's six tabs are 0.9-1.3 mm from J1-J4, inside JLC's 1.5 mm tab keep-out (https://jlcpcb.com/blog/pcb-mouse-bites); snapping them bends the connector joints.
findings.action: Move the Frontend's south tabs to another edge and order ±0.1 mm outline routing. Move FPGA-LDO A's tabs at least 1.5 mm from J1-J4.

findings.title: There is no grounding plan for eight stacks on one animal.
findings.why: If the stacks share one head ground, supply return current (milliamps) runs through ASIC AGND and the recording reference, so load steps can put up to about 13 mV on a reference that records microvolt signals. The animal is also tied to the PC and 12 V adapter ground with no isolation or leakage rule.
findings.action: Before ordering FPGA-LDO A, decide where the animal ground attaches (ASIC J1 is no longer fitted) and add a GND strap pad to each head board. Test two powered stacks in saline. Write down the earth and leakage rule for the rig.

findings.title: The connectors are unkeyed, so an ASIC board can mate turned 180°.
findings.why: A turned ASIC board puts ±8 V onto ASIC clock and data pins and would likely destroy the bonded ASICs. Housing is set aside, but this one can kill the chips.
findings.action: Add a key, or at least an orientation mark that stays visible after mating, and an orientation check in the bring-up steps.

findings.title: All eight ASICs share the stimulation control lines, and their settings cannot be read back.
findings.why: A chip that powers up with its stimulators enabled will stimulate whenever any chip in the stack does, and nothing can detect it.
findings.action: Ask the ASIC designer what the stimulation registers hold after power-up and CHIP_RESET. Make it a firmware rule to load an all-off table into all eight chips after every power-up and reset, before STIM_EN goes high.

findings.title: There is no bring-up procedure, and a stacked head has no test points.
findings.why: The first power-up of bonded ASICs depends on remembering scattered rules, and one missed step can destroy all eight ASICs of a head. Once stacked, the rails and signals cannot be probed.
findings.action: Write a one-page order: HDMI board alone; Frontend alone; Frontend + FPGA-LDO without ASIC boards (check all nine rails); bare ASIC boards; bonded boards last, cable on last.

findings.title: The cable data rate is not set, and the only recorded rate (1.25 Gb/s) is too slow for eight ASICs.
findings.why: Each cable's one GT lane carries all eight ASICs of a stack, and eight stacks need PCIe Gen3 x4 with packed samples at the PC.
findings.action: Record the lane rate and framing (for example 2.5 Gb/s with packed data). Run an IBERT eye test over one real cable, and check Gen3 x4 training through the Thunderbolt adapter.

findings.title: No cable is chosen, and a thin cable can push a stack into the 637 mA port limit.
findings.why: A high-load stack on a 1.8 m cable with 30-32 AWG power wire reaches the limit and the Frontend browns out. JTAG TMS uses HDMI pin 2, which some cables leave out, and the plug must be under about 9.2 mm thick and 13 mm wide.
findings.action: Write a cable spec (Micro-HDMI both ends, all 19 pins wired, 5 V loop under about 0.9 Ω, plug size) and measure a sample.

findings.title: Head heat is not estimated or limited.
findings.why: About 1.45 W per stack gives a 19-34 K surface rise in still air, and the commercial-grade FPGA is rated only to 85 °C (DS181: https://docs.amd.com/v/u/en-US/ds181_Artix_7_Data_Sheet).
findings.action: Set a head-surface temperature limit and measure one powered stack running the real bitstream.

findings.title: Each port's 44 ASIC outputs return through only two ground contacts.
findings.why: Digital return current can flow into the analog ground and the reference, adding noise to every recording and disturbing the returned clocks. Pin map V6 now uses the spare contacts, so ground cannot be added to this revision.
findings.action: Measure AGND-DGND noise and recording noise on the first stack. If it is too high, add ground contacts in the next ASIC/LDO revision.

findings.title: The enclosure has no room for the XEM8310's heat sink.
findings.why: The 10-15 W module would run without a heat sink or fan in a closed box and may exceed its 70 °C rating.
findings.action: Decide whether FANSINK-05 is fitted, measure its height, and cut the lid or add a fan opening. Then measure the box temperature with the real bitstream.
